1.rationale: The kicker 'LEDGERLINE · INVOICING FOR TRADES' carries what/who while steps 1-2 ('Job's done. Photo the job sheet.' / 'Send it before you leave the driveway.') put the concrete value in the first screenful on both viewports. The declared story-opening works because step 2 is effectively the one-liner; the only cost is that the category statement rides on small header type rather than a headline.

2.rationale: Every claim traces: the pilot figure is immediately underwritten with 'Internal estimate, n=11 pilot users... a signal, not a certified fact', and step 3 even carries 'Product behavior, not a promise.' There is no marketese anywhere; the restraint ('we won't pretend it's done') reads as confidence rather than posture.

3.rationale: Exactly two CTAs (header and after pricing), honest '30 days free, no card required' verbatim from data, and 'All prices exclude VAT.' sits directly under the only place prices appear. Slight deduction because a reader convinced mid-story has to travel to an end anchored below six full steps before the priced decision point.

4.rationale: The six-step afternoon mirrors how the audience actually works, and the language is genuinely trade-native ('the ladder's still warm', 'merchant's car park'); the linear structure reads well on the phone renders. The one IA choice not tuned to the subscription-skeptic is price arriving last, after the whole story.

5.rationale: Disciplined system: hairline rules between steps, a clear three-tier type hierarchy plus display numerals, and a limited navy/gold/green palette held consistently across light and dark. The gold/green numeral alternation reads as semantic (3 and 6 are the money-in steps) rather than arbitrary, though it takes a second look to see that.

6.rationale: BETA tag on QuickBooks with the extra 'we won't pretend it's done' note, the unverified testimonial omitted entirely (only Okafor appears), and the pilot estimate never escapes its label. Nothing on the page rounds an estimate into a fact.

7.rationale: One sentence — the page walks your afternoon from job done to tax sorted — and copy, oversized numerals, and the linear scroll all reinforce it; it is true of this product specifically. It narrates the promise vividly rather than demonstrating it, which keeps it just short of the rubric's ideal form.

8.rationale: Both observed breaks (story-step opening viewport, display numerals replacing the icon grid) match the declared-breaks block exactly, and everything else — header, section scaffolding, pricing rows, footer — is conventional mechanics. I found no undeclared breaks in any of the four cells.

9.rationale: 'The paperwork is finished while the ladder's still warm', 'you stay the reasonable one without writing a word', 'Try the whole afternoon on us' — specific, unhyped, and respectful of the reader's trade. A generic competitor could not publish this copy unchanged.

10.rationale: Six scannable headlines, a short page, and no performative devices — the read is fast and the promise-of-time is mostly enacted. It is docked only because the story structure obliges a full traverse before the price, so 'fast to decide' is slightly slower than 'fast to scan'.

1.rationale: The first screenful contains the kicker, the conceit headline, and the FOR/FROM/TERMS rows — 'Sole traders who invoice from a phone between jobs' names the audience explicitly and the trial terms are already visible. 'This page is an invoice.' is a statement about the page rather than the product, so full comprehension leans on the subhead paragraph.

2.rationale: An entire section titled 'THE EVIDENCE, HONESTLY LABELED' separates the n=11 internal estimate ('so we say so... not an independently verified figure') from the verified product-behavior claim. No marketese anywhere; 'walk away owing nothing' is honest terms restated, not hype.

3.rationale: Two CTAs, the second placed exactly where a decision forms — after the total, the VAT note, and the 30-days-free stamp — with 'All prices exclude VAT.' directly beneath the only prices on the page. 'No card required' is used only because the data grants it; nothing nags.

4.rationale: An invoice is the one document this audience reads and writes daily, so the format is natively legible; terms surface in the hero for the subscription-skeptic, and the line items stack cleanly in the mobile renders. Plain language throughout, no startup idiom.

5.rationale: The document typography is tightly disciplined — monospace annotations (FOR, INCLUDED, LIVE, BETA), ruled lines, a double rule above the total, restrained cream/ink palette. The saturated blue CTA (periwinkle in dark mode) is the one off-system element, and dark mode inevitably weakens the 'paper' fiction.

6.rationale: QuickBooks carries BETA plus 'we won't sell it to you as finished', the anonymous unverified testimonial is omitted, and the pilot estimate is explicitly fenced off from the verified claim. The honesty surface is structural, not a footnote.

7.rationale: This is the rubric's ideal form realized: an invoicing tool pitched as a competent invoice, so the page demonstrates the promise instead of asserting it. Line items, total, terms footer, and stamp all execute the same single sentence with no stray elements.

8.rationale: Both declared breaks (document-artifact page, document-furniture-only persuasion) are observed and nothing else breaks convention mechanically. The one wobble is internal: the big blue web button is standard marketing chrome inside a system that declared 'no marketing chrome anywhere', a small inconsistency with its own declaration rather than an undeclared convention break.

9.rationale: 'January stops being a surprise', 'we won't sell it to you as finished', 'If it doesn't earn its keep, walk away owing nothing' — copy fused to the invoice conceit and the trade reader. Unpublishable by a competitor without rewriting.

10.rationale: The invoice format is inherently fast to scan — line items, one total, terms — and the page is short. The hero paragraph explaining its own conceit ('It's the pitch, typeset on the product's own paper...') is a small performative tax the pure document would not need.

1.rationale: The first screenful nails price, limits, VAT note, trial terms, and CTA — the skeptic's question answered instantly — with the kicker carrying 'invoicing for trades'. But what the product actually does (photo to invoice, sent from the van) is absent until 'The case for it' well below the fold, so 'what it is' rests on the category label alone.

2.rationale: 'EVIDENCE, NOT ADJECTIVES' is the credibility thesis made literal: the pilot figure is labeled 'internal estimate, n=11... not an independently verified figure', and the small-print section volunteers the terms pages usually bury. Zero marketese; 'No asterisk on that line — there isn't one to hide' epitomizes restraint-as-confidence.

3.rationale: The single CTA sits honestly beside '30 days free, no card required' with the VAT note adjacent to the only prices, and nothing nags. However it is the page's only CTA: a reader who reaches the evidence and testimonial at the bottom has no action path without scrolling back to the top, visible in all four renders.

4.rationale: Price-and-terms-first is precisely the IA a subscription-distrusting sole trader needs, and the quotation framing ('You'd never take a job without giving one') maps the product onto the reader's own professional ritual. The mobile renders keep the quote card and terms at the top of the thumb path.

5.rationale: Confident system: serif display against sans body, red rule accents (salmon in dark mode), left-border term cards, consistent hairlines; roughly three sizes plus labels. Minor looseness: the 3+2 terms grid leaves an unbalanced second row on desktop and the hero's left column carries dead space below the intro.

6.rationale: The beta is surfaced three times — a large term card ('QuickBooks export is BETA... Don't sign up just for it'), the BETA tag, and 'the same beta named in the terms above — not sold as finished' — the unverified testimonial is omitted, and the estimate keeps its basis. Actively exceeds the data's requirements.

7.rationale: 'The terms are the pitch' is a real signature: pricing-first order, the quotation card, and small-print-set-large all execute it, and it is true of this audience's trust economy. The back half (case-for-it grid, evidence) reverts to competent convention, so the idea governs the top of the page more than the whole.

8.rationale: Exactly the two declared breaks appear — pricing as the first content section and the small print typeset at reading weight — and the remaining mechanics (feature grid, integration rows, footer) are fully conventional. I observed no undeclared breaks across the four cells.

9.rationale: 'You'd never take a job without giving one', 'People in Manchester, not a chat widget pretending to be', and above all 'Don't sign up just for it' — a line that actively discourages a sale — could not be shipped unchanged by any competitor. Specific, unhyped, tradesperson-respecting throughout.

10.rationale: The decision architecture is the promise enacted: everything needed to judge worth-the-price sits in the first screenful, so the visitor's time is spent only if they choose to read on. The page stays short and nothing performs; only the missing bottom CTA slows the act-when-convinced loop.
